- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring or one-time remote agent ("run this every Monday", "open a cleanup PR for X in 2 weeks"), or to manage existing routines. ALSO OFFER PROACTIVELY: after you finish work that has a natural future follow-up, end your reply with a one-line offer to schedule a background agent to do it. Strong signals: a feature flag / gate / experiment / staged rollout was just shipped (offer a one-time agent in ~2 weeks to open a cleanup PR or evaluate results), a new alert/monitor was created (offer a recurring agent to triage it), a TODO/migration with a "remove once X" condition was left behind (offer a one-time agent to do the removal). Skip the offer for refactors, bug fixes, and anything that is done once it ships. Name a concrete action and cadence ("in 2 weeks", "every Monday") and only offer when the run just succeeded — do not pitch a schedule for something that has not happened yet.
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text:
Good timing — I've now read all the relevant files. Here's my thinking on each area:

---

## Assets & Entities

The current tab does a lot — physical components, world entities, AI image generation, property panels, entity-to-rule linking — but it all flows linearly top-to-bottom without much visual hierarchy. Some ideas:

- **Split-panel layout**: Left column is a collapsible entity/asset browser (grouped by type, searchable), right panel shows the full detail view for the selected item — similar to how a code editor or Finder works. Right now editing and browsing fight for the same vertical space.
- **Promoted property panel**: Entity properties (`EntityProperty`) are powerful but feel buried. A dedicated "Stats & Attributes" section within each entity detail — similar to how Assets already has a multi-field status/kind system — would make this more visible.
- **Component map**: A visual "canvas" view (toggle from list view) showing all components as cards laid out by category, so you can see the full component inventory at a glance without scrolling.
- **Cross-links surfaced on the card**: Each entity card could show a small inline "Linked rules: 2, Linked assets: 1" count that's clickable, rather than having to expand and scroll. Entity-to-rule linking exists in the data layer but isn't prominent in the UI.

---

## Rules — Markdown / Rulebook View

Your instinct is right — individual sandbox cards are great for iteration but terrible for understanding how rules *fit together* as a system. Ideas:

- **Dual-mode toggle**: a "Sandbox" mode (current card view, good for AI iteration and conflict checking) and a **"Rulebook" mode** — a live Markdown document that assembles rules into sections by category with proper headings, paragraph flow, and numbered clauses.
- **Inline MD editor**: The Rulebook view would be an actual editable Markdown textarea (rendered with something like `react-markdown` + `remark`) — so rules can have headers like `## 3. Combat` with sub-rules listed below them. Each section maps to a category.
- **Auto-generated table of contents**: Derived from category groupings, so the designer can see the full structure at a glance — "does my rulebook have gaps?"
- **Completeness scoring**: A small sidebar metric — "Rules cover: Movement ✓, Combat ✓, Win Conditions ✗, Setup ✗" — using AI to flag structural holes rather than just individual card conflicts.
- **Export-ready**: The MD view doubles as the export source for the Exports tab, so the rules actually look like a document someone could hand to a playtester.

---

## Players Tab

Compared to Assets & Entities — which has subtypes, custom properties, status tracking, AI image generation, and rule linking — Players is relatively shallow: name, type, role, description, strategy. Ideas to bring it up to parity:

- **Stat blocks**: A key-value property system (just like `EntityProperty` for Entities) — HP, Speed, Attack, Defense, special attributes. Could be freeform or templated by player type.
- **Linked abilities and factions**: Players currently have no connection to the `Ability` or `Faction` entity types. A small linked-entities row on the player card (matching the LinkedEntitiesBar pattern from Rules) would tie the data model together.
- **Relationship map**: A small visual diagram showing "Character A is allied with NPC B, opposed to Enemy C" — especially useful for narrative-heavy games. Could be a simple force-directed graph.
- **Playbook section**: Expand "Strategy" into a richer section — maybe AI-generated decision trees, encounter behaviors, or loot tables for enemies/bosses.
- **Portrait/art slot**: The same AI image generation pipeline that Assets uses (component art) could be available here for character portraits.

---

## Research Tab

Currently a flat card grid — title, URL, notes, tags. It works but doesn't connect research back to the design. Ideas:

- **Category system** replacing free-form tags: "Mechanical Inspiration", "Theme Reference", "Competitor Analysis", "Playtest Feedback", "Market Research" — with color-coded lanes like the Rules categories.
- **Link research to specific rules or entities**: A "inspired by" trail — clicking a rule could show which research items influenced it, and vice versa. This makes the design reasoning traceable.
- **AI Synthesis button**: Takes all tagged research items and asks the AI "what patterns are emerging here? What design direction is implied?" — a higher-level insight pass rather than per-card enhancement.
- **Board / kanban view**: Research items as swimlane columns by category rather than a flat grid — easier to spot imbalances (e.g. "all my research is mechanical, nothing thematic").
- **Timestamps and design phase annotations**: Show when each item was added relative to the current design phase, so you can see how research evolved alongside the project.

---

## Board Game Shelf (Reference Games)

Currently lives in **Overview** as the "Reference games" card. The right new home is **Research** — semantically, reference games ARE a form of research (competitor/inspiration analysis). 

In Research it could get its own promoted section at the top: a dedicated "Reference Shelf" block, visually distinct from individual sources (maybe even a card-style shelf layout with box-art placeholders), with the "borrowing / avoiding" fields intact. This would also let the Research tab auto-query BGG or Wikipedia for basic info when a game name is entered — title, year, mechanic tags — saving the designer from manually describing it.

---

**Short version**: Rules needs a document-layer on top of the sandbox, Players needs the same depth as Assets, Research needs categories + cross-links, the shelf moves there naturally, and Assets benefits most from a split-panel detail view. Want me to start on any of these?

aiTitle: Improve UI tabs and research organization

content.text:
Now I have a complete picture. Here's my thinking across all of these:

---

## Spreadsheet View for Entities

The current `EntityProperties` panel (`assets-entities.tsx:1955`) already has a table-like grid but it only shows *one entity's properties at a time* — one row per property. The problem is when you have 60 cards in a deck or 100 tiles in Azul's bag, you need the inverse: **one row per entity, one column per property**.

What I'd add:

- **Toggle between Card view and Sheet view** at the top of EntitiesView. Sheet view renders all entities as a spreadsheet — rows are entities, columns are: Name, Type, Subtype, and then every `EntityProperty` key that exists across that entity type.
- **Inline cell editing** — click a cell, edit in place, Tab to next. No dialog required.
- **Bulk row add** — "+ Add 10 rows" that creates blank entity stubs you fill in. Critical for Skip-Bo (144 cards) or Azul (100 tiles).
- **CSV import/export** — paste from Google Sheets / Excel directly. This is a huge workflow win for designers who already have their card list in a spreadsheet.
- **Column pinning** — pin Name, freeze the left column while scrolling right through custom properties.
- **Computed/formula columns** — read-only columns derived from others. For a combat game: `Power = Attack + Defense`. These don't need to be stored, just displayed.

The key data model gap: right now entities don't have a `quantity` field — assets do, but entities don't. For Azul's tiles, the entity IS the tile type ("Blue Tile") and quantity belongs on it (20). That needs to be a first-class entity field, not just an asset field.

---

## Card Text & Deck Contents

This is the biggest gap. When you define a Deck entity, there's no place to define what's *inside* it. The Gamma prompt builder (`buildDeckPrompt`) already knows this structure exists conceptually but the data layer and UI don't surface it.

What I'd build:

- **Deck → Cards parent/child relationship**: When you expand a Deck entity in the Sheet view, it shows its child Card entities as nested rows. A "Cards in this deck" expandable section in the card view too.
- **Card Studio panel**: Click into a Deck → a dedicated panel opens showing all cards in the deck as a spreadsheet. Columns: Name, Subtype, Cost/Value, Effect Text, Flavor Text, Quantity in Deck, Art Description. This maps exactly to what a physical card would need.
- **AI batch generation for card text**: A text prompt like *"Generate 20 action cards for a dungeon-crawl deck — mix attack, defense, and event cards"* → AI fills in the full spreadsheet with names, effects, and flavor text. More powerful than the current one-at-a-time approach.
- **Card text templates per subtype**: Each subtype (Action, Item, Spell, Event) has a different field schema. An Action card has "Cost + Effect"; an Event card has "Trigger + Duration + Effect". Templates enforce consistent structure across the deck.
- **Card preview panel**: Side panel showing a rough layout of how the text would sit on the card — title bar, effect box, flavor text in italics — not fully rendered art but enough to catch "the text is too long for this card".
- **Quantity-aware totals**: Bottom of deck spreadsheet shows total card count, quantity-weighted (if you have 3 copies of "Goblin Attack" it counts as 3, not 1).

---

## Broadening Beyond Card/Deck Games

The current framing is card-game-centric even though the component types theoretically support everything. Here's how I'd think about each:

**Azul (tile drafting, pattern placement)**
- Components: Tile (5 color variants × 20 = 100), Factory display board (Player board), Scoring track (Board), Center pool (abstract zone)
- What's missing: **Color-variant system** — Blue Tile and Yellow Tile are the same entity type but different colors with exact quantities. Right now you'd have to make 5 separate Token/Tile entities and manually set quantity to 20 each. A "Variant set" feature on a component type (name: "Azul Tile", variants: Blue/Yellow/Red/Black/White, quantity each: 20) would make this natural.
- The pattern grid (wall) on the player board needs a **grid designer tool** — a visual N×N grid where you can mark which cell takes which color. That's specific to Azul-style games.

**Heat: Pedal to the Metal (racing, gear+deck management)**
- Components: Speed cards (deck, values 1-6), Heat cards (deck), Upgrade cards, Track tiles (modular hex/curve pieces), Dashboard, Gear marker, Car token
- What's missing: **Modular track/tile sequencer** — a tool to lay out tile pieces in order to form a circuit. Think of it as a tile editor where tiles chain together with connection points. Also **numeric card values** as a first-class property (not just subtype) so the deck statistics (avg speed, heat distribution) can be calculated.

**Pirate's Dice / Liar's Dice (dice + bluffing)**
- Components: 5 dice per player, cups
- Extremely component-light. What matters is the **die face designer** — custom dice where you define what's on each of the 6 faces, with icons or values. Also a **probability table** in the Simulator: given N dice, what's the probability of exactly K sixes?
- The current Die type exists as an entity but has no face definition tool.

**Skip-Bo (card sequencing, hand management)**
- Components: 162 cards (numbers 1–12, plus 18 Skip-Bo wild cards), discard piles, building piles
- Almost entirely handled by the spreadsheet view — a numbered card set is just rows in a table. The missing piece is **pile/zone modeling**: modeling game zones (draw pile, discard pile, building piles, stockpile, hand) as first-class design concepts, not just implied by the rules text. A "Zone Map" component — named zones with their properties (shared/private, face-up/face-down, max size) — would serve Skip-Bo, Solitaire, and any hand-management game.

**Universal needs across all these:**
- Remove the assumption that every game has cards. A project tagged as "Tile Placement" shouldn't show Deck-specific tools prominently.
- Game type tagging at project creation should pre-configure which entity types, tools, and templates are surfaced.
- "Zone modeling" (draw pile, bag, discard, board areas) as a component concept.
- A **component manifest / bill of materials** view — total component count across the entire game with quantities. Azul's reads: 100 tiles, 5 factory boards, 1 center display, 4 player boards, 1 scoring track, 1 bag. This is also the thing you hand to a manufacturer.

---

## Monopoly as the Training / Reference Game

This is exactly the right instinct. Monopoly is universally known, component-rich, and mechanically diverse — it's the best possible worked example.

**How Monopoly maps to GameForge's data model:**

| GameForge Type | Monopoly Component |
|---|---|
| Board | The main 40-space board |
| Tile | Individual board spaces (Go, Jail, Free Parking, Properties) |
| Card | Chance cards (16), Community Chest cards (16) |
| Deck | Chance deck, Community Chest deck |
| Token (Meeple) | Player tokens (top hat, car, dog…) |
| Token (Resource) | Money — $1, $5, $10, $20, $50, $100, $500 denominations |
| Token | Houses (32), Hotels (12) |
| Die | 2 standard d6 |
| Faction | Color groups (Brown, Light Blue, Pink, Orange, Red, Yellow, Green, Dark Blue) |
| Resource | Individual property deed cards |
| Entity Property | Purchase price, rent tiers ×6, mortgage value, build cost |

That's every single entity type used, which is why it's the perfect training example.

**What I'd build around this:**

- A **"Demo: Monopoly"** pre-built project that ships with the app — all entities defined, key rules written, turn structure set. Users can explore a real game as a reference instead of building from scratch. This also doubles as a stress test of every feature.
- The **Learn section** (which I saw references `design-101.tsx`) should have a dedicated "Deconstruct a game" module using Monopoly — "here's every decision Hasbro made and why, mapped to GameForge concepts."
- The AI chat should have Monopoly in its system context when the user hasn't defined their own reference games yet — so early suggestions are grounded in something concrete.
- A **"Model a game you know"** onboarding path: pick Monopoly (or Catan, or Chess) → see how it's structured → use that as the starting point for your own design.

---

## What Else I'd Add

A few more ideas that fall out of all this:

**Component Bill of Materials (BOM) view** — a manufacturing-focused table: every component, its type, quantity, dimensions, and a rough unit-cost tier (cheap: dice/tokens, medium: cards, expensive: custom boards). For any designer thinking about publishing, "how much will this cost to make 1000 copies?" is an early critical question. This could live in the Exports tab.

**Zone Map** — as mentioned above, a named-zone system (Draw Pile, Discard, Hand, Board Zone A, Bag) with properties (public/private, ordered/unordered, face-up/face-down, capacity). This makes hand-management, drafting, and bag-building games model naturally without forcing everything into deck metaphors.

**Die Face Designer** — a simple die face editor: 6 faces, each with a value or icon. Used for custom dice in games like King of Tokyo, Roll for the Galaxy, or any game with custom dice mechanics. Feeds directly into the Simulator's probability calculations.

**Blind Playtest Export** — a read-only, shareable web link or PDF of just the rules and component list. No editor UI, no AI panels — just what a playtester needs. This is distinct from the current Exports tab which feels more asset-download focused.

**Complexity Score** — a real-time estimate derived from rule count, entity count, property depth, player count range, and turn phase count — output as a 1–5 complexity tier (BGG scale equivalent) with a breakdown of which factors are driving it up. Useful for positioning your game in the market.

**Quick Reference Card generator** — a 2-sided half-page player aid, auto-generated from rules + turn structure. Every hobbyist-published game needs one. Could be the first thing coming out of the Exports tab for any game type.

---

**Short version**: the spreadsheet view and deck card studio are the highest-value near-term additions. Monopoly as a demo project is a cheap, high-leverage feature that makes every other tool immediately understandable. The broadening to non-card games mostly requires zone modeling, component variant/quantity system, and removing card-first assumptions from the UI. Want to start implementing any of these?

export interface LearnTopic {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  context: string;
}

const T = (id: string, title: string, context: string): LearnTopic => ({
  id,
  title,
  context: context.trim(),
});

export const LEARN_TOPICS: Record<string, LearnTopic> = Object.fromEntries(
  [
    T(
      "bible:welcome",
      "Welcome to GameForge",
      `GameForge is an end-to-end IDE for designing tabletop games. The core loop is: brainstorm with the AI Co-Designer, define entities & rules, simulate with Monte Carlo and live playthroughs, generate assets, and export print-and-play files. The Bible introduces this loop. Confident designers should know which tab solves which problem and how to move work forward through the workflow rather than getting stuck in any one phase.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:overview",
      "Workspace overview",
      `The workspace is organized into tabs: Research, Ontology, Entities, Players, Rules, Simulator, Assets, Playtesting, Notes, Tasks, Storyboard, Balance, Exports, Chat, and AI Providers. Tabs share project state via Drizzle/Postgres so changes propagate. Designers should understand which tabs are upstream (Research, Ontology) vs. downstream (Simulator, Exports) and not skip the early definitional work.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:research",
      "Research tab",
      `Research is where you collect inspirations, references to existing games, mechanics catalog, and target audience notes. It informs everything downstream. Confident designers do landscape analysis (what plays well in this genre? what's overdone?) and write a one-paragraph design pillar before touching mechanics. Use research to pre-empt "this already exists" feedback.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:ontology",
      "Ontology tab",
      `Ontology defines the conceptual schema of your game: which kinds of things exist (Cards, Tokens, Resources, Locations, Players, Phases) and how they relate. Good ontologies are minimal — fewer entity types means clearer rules. Confident designers iterate on ontology before authoring entities; a messy ontology produces messy rules.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:entities",
      "Entities tab",
      `Entities are concrete instances of your ontology types: specific cards, tokens, board tiles, decks. The Entities tab supports bulk editing, tagging, and balance metadata (cost, power, rarity). Confident designers define entity templates first (e.g. "all attack cards have cost, damage, range") so balance work and asset generation can be automated downstream.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:players",
      "Players tab",
      `Players defines player counts, personas, win conditions per player, and asymmetric roles if any. Confident designers explicitly model archetype players ("the optimizer", "the storyteller", "the new player") and check that core decisions remain interesting for each archetype. Player counts have huge implications for downtime, scaling, and table presence.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:rules",
      "Rules tab",
      `Rules captures the rulebook in structured form: setup, turn structure, phases, actions, end conditions, edge cases, and FAQ. Confident designers write rules as a state machine (phases → legal actions → state changes) and aggressively cut special cases. Each special case is a tax on every future playtest.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:simulator",
      "Simulator tab",
      `Simulator runs Monte Carlo trials and live agent playthroughs against your current rules. It surfaces game length, win rate skew, kingmaker scenarios, and dead strategies. Confident designers tune simulator agents to specific personas and read variance — high variance can mean exciting OR broken; you have to inspect runs to know which.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:assets",
      "Assets tab",
      `Assets generates and manages card art, tokens, board art, icons, and tuckbox graphics using AI image models, with templates that bind to your entity data so a card's text/cost/art update together. Confident designers lock template layout early and defer "final art" until rules are stable; cheap placeholder art keeps focus on play.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:playtesting",
      "Playtesting tab",
      `Playtesting tracks scheduled sessions, participants, structured feedback forms, and notes against specific rules versions. Confident designers run blind tests (no designer at the table), instrument with observation sheets (decisions, downtime, rules questions), and triage feedback into "fix-now / iterate / not-a-bug" rather than reacting to every comment.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:notes",
      "Notes tab",
      `Notes is freeform markdown for half-formed ideas, design journal entries, and meeting notes. Treat it as your scratch space; it's not graded by simulator or rules. Confident designers periodically promote good notes into Rules, Tasks, or Research entries instead of letting them rot.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:tasks",
      "Tasks tab",
      `Tasks is a lightweight backlog — design debts, balance issues, art todos, rule clarifications — with priority and status. Confident designers keep this list short and ruthlessly close stale items; a 200-task backlog is a graveyard, not a plan.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:storyboard",
      "Storyboard tab",
      `Storyboard sequences key moments of a typical game: the opening, the mid-game pivot, the climax, the resolution. It's a narrative-design tool that exposes pacing problems. Confident designers use it to verify that the game has a discernible arc rather than 90 minutes of uniform turns.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:balance",
      "Balance tab",
      `Balance aggregates simulator output and exposes per-entity statistics — pick rates, win rates, win-rate-when-picked, average cost-to-impact ratios. Confident designers focus on outliers and look for "dominant" or "trap" cards; perfect balance is impossible, but extreme outliers should be either nerfed/buffed or made deliberately powerful with a clear cost.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:exports",
      "Exports tab",
      `Exports produces print-and-play PDFs, Tabletop Simulator mods, and manufacturer-ready files (bleed, CMYK, DPI). Confident designers treat exports as a checkpoint — a clean export forces you to confront missing icons, untested copy, and incomplete entity data.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:chat",
      "Project chat",
      `Project chat is the workspace-wide AI Co-Designer that has access to your entire project state — all tabs, entities, rules. Use it for cross-cutting design questions ("does my deck composition support my win condition?"). It is distinct from the topic-scoped tutor inside Learn, which only knows about one chapter at a time.`,
    ),
    T(
      "bible:ai-providers",
      "AI providers",
      `AI Providers lets a workspace admin choose which LLM/image providers power Co-Designer, Tutor, Simulator agents, and Asset generation. Different providers have different strengths (reasoning, speed, image style) and cost profiles. Confident designers pick a fast cheap model for ideation and a stronger model for rule synthesis or balance critique.`,
    ),

    T(
      "design101:01-what-is",
      "What is a board game, really?",
      `A board game is a structured social experience produced by rules, components, and players — not just the rulebook. The "feeling" the game produces (tension, laughter, satisfying optimization, story) is the product. Confident designers write a one-sentence pitch ("a 60-minute negotiation game where every alliance must betray someone") and a one-line target feeling, then constantly check decisions against both.`,
    ),
    T(
      "design101:02-goals",
      "Goals, win conditions, and player motivation",
      `Win conditions tell players what to optimize. They can be single-axis (most VP), multi-axis (any of 3 paths), variable (asymmetric goals), or absent (sandbox). Motivation also comes from non-victory rewards: storytelling, mastery, expression. Confident designers ensure the dominant strategy is interesting, that there is more than one viable path, and that catch-up mechanics don't punish good play.`,
    ),
    T(
      "design101:03-mechanics",
      "Mechanics: the verbs of your game",
      `Mechanics are the verbs players do: draft, bid, place, move, push-your-luck, area-control, set-collection, deck-build, worker-placement, roll-and-write. Each mechanic has a "feel" and constraints. Confident designers pick 1-2 core mechanics and 1-2 supporting ones; combining 5+ unrelated mechanics produces incoherent games. Mechanics should reinforce the target feeling.`,
    ),
    T(
      "design101:04-components",
      "Components and physical design",
      `Components are the physical UI: cards, dice, boards, tokens, player aids. They communicate state, constrain action space, and create tactile pleasure. Confident designers minimize component count, give every component a clear "language" (color, shape, icon), and prototype with paper before committing to manufacturing. Player aids are not optional — they are the rulebook compressed.`,
    ),
    T(
      "design101:05-balance",
      "Balance and probability",
      `Balance is about keeping decisions interesting, not about making everything equal. Use expected value, variance, and dominant-strategy analysis. Common heuristics: cost-to-impact roughly linear; no card is strictly better than another; variance is okay if it creates stories. Confident designers compute EV by hand for at least the top 5 cards, then verify with simulation.`,
    ),
    T(
      "design101:06-iteration",
      "Iteration and playtesting culture",
      `Design is iteration. Build the cheapest playable thing, test, learn, change one variable, retest. Confident designers separate "this rule is broken" from "this player didn't like this rule"; small samples lie. Use blind tests once you think you have a candidate, and freeze rules between rounds of testing so you can attribute changes.`,
    ),
    T(
      "design101:07-theme",
      "Theme and narrative integration",
      `Theme is the fiction wrapped around mechanics; integration means mechanics feel like the fiction. "Pasted-on" themes can be swapped without changing play; integrated themes can't. Confident designers either commit to deep integration (every mechanic justified by fiction) or lean into abstract elegance — half-measures feel worst.`,
    ),
    T(
      "design101:08-publishing",
      "Publishing paths and going to market",
      `You can self-publish (Kickstarter, direct), license to a publisher, or sell as print-and-play. Each path has different time, money, and creative-control trade-offs. Confident designers know roughly: self-pub needs ~$30k-$100k for a print run and a marketing audience; licensing needs a polished prototype and a pitch; PnP earns little but builds reputation.`,
    ),
  ].map((t) => [t.id, t]),
);

export function getLearnTopic(id: string): LearnTopic | undefined {
  return LEARN_TOPICS[id];
}

- **Assets view**: Manage images, concept art, card mockups, and digital files
- **Components view**: Full entity management with Cards/Sheet toggle and per-entity tool panels

**Component types supported:**
- Card / Deck — Cards live inside Decks. Use Card Studio (expand any Deck entity) to manage individual cards, write card text, and AI-batch generate card content.
- Token — Resource, currency, health, status markers. Supports color/variant manager (e.g. Azul's 5 colors × 20 tiles each).
- Tile — Map, dungeon, terrain. Tile entities also get the variant manager for color/region sets.
- Die — Custom dice. Each Die entity gets the Die Face Designer: edit all 6 faces with emoji or text, see probability distribution.
- Meeple — Pawns, figures, standees, miniatures.
- Board — Game boards, player mats, reference sheets.
- Zone — Draw pile, discard pile, hand, market, bag, supply. Zones model game flow topology — where cards go between states.
- Location / Faction / Event / Resource / Ability — Conceptual world-building types (no physical component; filtered out of the BOM).

**Sheet view**: A spreadsheet-style table for bulk-editing entity names, types, subtypes, descriptions. Supports CSV import/export.

**Card Studio**: Expanded inside any Deck entity. Shows all child cards, allows individual editing, and uses AI batch generation with automatic parent assignment.

**Die Face Designer**: Edit face_1 through face_6, choose emoji from a quick palette, see face distribution as probability bars.

**Variant Manager**: For Tile and Token entities — define named color/variant sets with quantities (e.g. "Blue: 20, Red: 20, Yellow: 20").`,

`You can self-publish (Kickstarter, direct), license to a publisher, or sell as print-and-play. Each path has different time, money, and creative-control trade-offs. Confident designers know roughly: self-pub needs ~$30k-$100k for a print run and a marketing audience; licensing needs a polished prototype and a pitch; PnP earns little but builds reputation.`,
    ),

    T(
      "tools:card-studio",
      "Card Studio — deck and card management",
      `Card Studio is the card-management panel inside any Deck entity in the Assets & Entities tab (expand a Deck entity to access it).

**What it does:**
- Lists all child cards assigned to the deck with their name, subtype, description, and lore
- Lets you add individual cards manually
- AI batch generation: enter a count and prompt, click Generate. GameForge generates that many Card entities, then automatically assigns them to the parent Deck via parentEntityId. This works around the AI API limitation — entities are generated first, then reparented.
- Inline editing: click any field on a card to edit it in place
- Delete individual cards

**Card data model:**
- name, type ("Card"), subtype (Action / Item / Spell / Event / etc.)
- description — the functional card text (what it does mechanically)
- lore — flavor text (thematic, optional)
- parentEntityId — the Deck entity's id that this card belongs to

**Good practice:**
- Define your card template (what fields each card uses) before generating in bulk
- Use the Sheet view for mass-edit after generation
- Check the BOM view — cards count toward the physical component total (each card = 1 unit; deck quantity = sum of child cards)`,
    ),
    T(
      "tools:die-face-designer",
      "Die Face Designer — custom dice",
      `The Die Face Designer appears when you expand a Die entity in the Assets & Entities tab.

**What it does:**
- Lets you define all 6 faces of a custom die using text or emoji
- Quick emoji palette with common game symbols (⚔️ 🛡️ 🏃 💎 ✨ 💀 🔥 ⚡ 🎯 🌟 ❌ ✅)
- Probability distribution: shows the percentage chance of each face being rolled (uniform for a d6, so each face = ~16.7%, but useful to compare how many faces share the same outcome)
- Dirty state detection: "Save faces" is only enabled when the face values differ from what is stored

**Storage**: Faces are stored as entity properties named face_1 through face_6 with textValue. This reuses the existing EntityProperty system with no schema changes.

**Game design notes:**
- For combat dice (like Eldritch Horror / Arkham Horror), group faces by outcome type: hits, misses, blanks, wilds
- For push-your-luck dice (e.g. Zombie Dice), the tension comes from face distribution — too many blanks → cautious play; too few → broken
- Probability display helps you catch unintended distributions before prototyping`,
    ),
    T(
      "tools:variant-manager",
      "Variant Manager — color and component sets",
      `The Variant Manager appears when you expand a Tile or Token entity in the Assets & Entities tab.

**What it does:**
- Defines named color/variant sets with per-variant quantities
- Running total shows overall component count across all variants
- Percentage bars show the distribution (useful for spotting uneven sets)
- Add, rename, and delete variants; adjust quantities inline

**Storage**: Variants are stored as entity properties with a "variant_" prefix (e.g. "variant_Blue" = 20, "variant_Red" = 20). The defaultValue field holds the integer quantity.

**Example — Azul:**
- Tile entity "Tile"
- Variants: Blue 20, Yellow 20, Red 20, Black 20, White 20
- Total: 100 tiles

**Example — Pirate's Dice:**
- Token entity "Skull Cup"
- Variants: White 30, Black 30
- (or model each player's dice set as a separate Token entity)

**Game design note**: Variant quantities feed into the BOM — the BOM currently shows 1 unit per top-level entity, but the Variant Manager helps you communicate the exact physical count to manufacturers and backers when writing the component list.`,
    ),
    T(
      "tools:zone-topology",
      "Zone entities — modeling game flow",
      `Zone is a special entity type in GameForge that models the locations where game elements move between states. Zones are physical (they take up table space or represent a conceptual holding area) but architectural — they define your game's flow topology before you write a single rule.

**Zone subtypes:**
- Draw Pile — where cards come from (face-down stack)
- Discard Pile — where used/spent cards go
- Hand — each player's private holding area
- Market — the face-up selection area (e.g. Dominion's market row)
- Board Area — a specific region on the board (e.g. a scoring track space)
- Supply — where tokens/resources are taken from
- Bag — randomized draw (tiles in a bag, Azul-style)
- Stockpile — a player's collected resources/cards

**Why model zones?**
Every card game has a state machine: cards move from Draw Pile → Hand → Play Area → Discard Pile → (shuffle) → Draw Pile. Modeling this as Zone entities forces you to be explicit about the cycle before rules are written, catching edge cases (what happens when the draw pile empties? is the discard reshuffled?).

**In the BOM**: Zones appear in the Physical Components table with tier "Reference Card" — model them as player-aid reference cards or board sections that label the zones.

**Example from Monopoly demo**: The Bank (Supply), Free Parking Pool (Board Area), and Player Hand (Hand) are all pre-loaded as Zone entities.`,
    ),
  ].map((t) => [t.id, t]),

- Defines named color/variant sets with per-variant quantities
- Running total shows overall component count across all variants
- Percentage bars show the distribution (useful for spotting uneven sets)
- Add, rename, and delete variants; adjust quantities inline

**Storage**: Variants are stored as entity properties with a "variant_" prefix (e.g. "variant_Blue" = 20, "variant_Red" = 20). The defaultValue field holds the integer quantity.

**Example — Azul:**
- Tile entity "Tile"
- Variants: Blue 20, Yellow 20, Red 20, Black 20, White 20
- Total: 100 tiles

**Example — Pirate's Dice:**
- Token entity "Skull Cup"
- Variants: White 30, Black 30
- (or model each player's dice set as a separate Token entity)

**Game design note**: Variant quantities feed into the BOM — the BOM currently shows 1 unit per top-level entity, but the Variant Manager helps you communicate the exact physical count to manufacturers and backers when writing the component list.`,

**Zone subtypes:**
- Draw Pile — where cards come from (face-down stack)
- Discard Pile — where used/spent cards go
- Hand — each player's private holding area
- Market — the face-up selection area (e.g. Dominion's market row)
- Board Area — a specific region on the board (e.g. a scoring track space)
- Supply — where tokens/resources are taken from
- Bag — randomized draw (tiles in a bag, Azul-style)
- Stockpile — a player's collected resources/cards

**Why model zones?**
Every card game has a state machine: cards move from Draw Pile → Hand → Play Area → Discard Pile → (shuffle) → Draw Pile. Modeling this as Zone entities forces you to be explicit about the cycle before rules are written, catching edge cases (what happens when the draw pile empties? is the discard reshuffled?).

**In the BOM**: Zones appear in the Physical Components table with tier "Reference Card" — model them as player-aid reference cards or board sections that label the zones.

# Monopoly — GameForge Rulebook

> Classic negotiation and property trading game. 2–8 players, 60–180 minutes.

**Type:** Board Game · **Genre:** Negotiation / Economic · **Players:** 2–8 · **Duration:** 60–180 min

---

## Objective

Be the last player remaining solvent. Force all opponents into bankruptcy by acquiring properties, building houses and hotels, and collecting rent whenever opponents land on your spaces.

**Tiebreaker:** If time is called, the player with the highest total net worth (cash + properties at purchase price + houses at $25 each + hotels at $50 each) wins.

## Components (27 total)

**Boards (1)**
- **Main Board** — 40-space board with properties, railroads, utilities, taxes, and corner spaces.

**Decks (2)**
- **Chance Deck** _(Event Deck)_ — 16 Chance cards with random positive and negative events.
- **Community Chest Deck** _(Event Deck)_ — 16 Community Chest cards with bank, neighbour, and jackpot events.

**Meeples (1)**
- **Player Tokens** _(Pawn)_ — 8 classic tokens: top hat, car, dog, thimble, iron, battleship, boot, wheelbarrow.

**Tokens (3)**
- **Monopoly Money** _(Currency)_ — Paper money in $1, $5, $10, $20, $50, $100, and $500 denominations.
- **Houses** _(Marker)_ — 32 green houses placed on owned properties to increase rent.
- **Hotels** _(Marker)_ — 12 red hotels — each replaces 4 houses on a property.

**Dice (1)**
- **Standard Dice** _(Action Die)_ — 2 standard d6 — roll both to move. Doubles roll again.

**Zones (3)**
- **Bank** _(Supply)_ — Unlimited money supply — pays salaries, loans, and holds unsold property deeds.
- **Free Parking Pool** _(Board Area)_ — Optional variant — taxes accumulate here and are collected by landing players.
- **Player Hand** _(Hand)_ — Each player holds their own property deeds, money, and Get Out of Jail Free cards.

**Conceptual (17)** — Property deed groups (Brown, Light Blue, Pink, Orange, Red, Yellow, Green, Dark Blue), Corner spaces (Go, Jail, Free Parking, Go to Jail), Special spaces (Tax Spaces, Railroads, Utilities), and Property Deeds resource.

---

## Setup

1. Place the **Main Board** in the center of the table.
2. Shuffle the **Chance Deck** and **Community Chest Deck** separately; place each face-down on their board spaces.
3. Each player chooses a **Player Token** and places it on **Go**.
4. The **Bank** distributes starting cash to each player: $1500 total (two $500s, two $100s, two $50s, six $20s, five $10s, five $5s, five $1s).
5. Remaining money, all **Property Deeds**, **Houses**, and **Hotels** stay with the Bank.
6. The player who rolls highest goes first. Play proceeds clockwise.

## Turn Order

Players take turns clockwise. On each turn a player **must** roll both dice and move their token the indicated number of spaces.

- **Rolling doubles**: Roll again immediately. Three consecutive doubles → go directly to Jail.
- **Jail**: A jailed player may not collect rent on unmortgaged properties. Exit by: rolling doubles on any of three turns, paying $50 bail before rolling, or using a Get Out of Jail Free card.

## Actions

**On your turn you may (in any order before/after rolling):**

**Buy Property**
When you land on an unowned property, you may buy it from the Bank at its listed price. If you decline, the Bank auctions it to the highest bidder (minimum $1).

**Collect Rent**
When an opponent lands on your property you must demand rent before the next player rolls. Rent is printed on the deed; it doubles when you own all properties of a colour group. Houses and hotels increase rent further (see deed card for tiers).

**Build Houses / Hotels**
If you own all properties in a colour group, you may buy houses ($25–$200 each depending on group) from the Bank and place them on your properties. Houses must be built evenly (no property in a group may have more than one house more than another). Four houses may be traded for one hotel.

**Mortgage**
Mortgage any unimproved property to the Bank for its mortgage value (half the purchase price). A mortgaged property pays no rent. Unmortgage by paying the mortgage value plus 10% interest.

**Trade**
At any time (including on other players' turns with mutual consent), players may trade properties, money, and Get Out of Jail Free cards. Future rent immunity cannot be traded.

**Draw Cards**
Landing on Chance or Community Chest spaces: draw the top card and follow its instructions. Return the card to the bottom of its deck when done (except Get Out of Jail Free cards, which are held until used or sold).

## Scoring

The game ends when all but one player are **bankrupt** (unable to pay a debt). A player who cannot pay must first mortgage properties and sell buildings to the Bank at half price. If still unable to pay, they are bankrupt and turn all remaining assets over to their creditor (or the Bank if the creditor is the Bank).

**The last player remaining is the winner.**

Optional timed game: after an agreed time, the player with the highest net worth wins.

---

## Glossary

**Monopoly** — Owning all properties in a colour group; doubles the base rent on all spaces in the group.
**Mortgage value** — Half the purchase price of a property; received when mortgaging, paid plus 10% to unmortgage.
**Rent** — The fee paid by a player who lands on another player's unmortgaged property.
**Bankruptcy** — The state of being unable to pay a debt even after liquidating all assets.
**Doubles** — Rolling the same number on both dice; grants an additional turn (and third doubles sends you to Jail).

---

content.text:
The Gamma document is live. Here's the full summary of everything that was built:

---

**Gamma doc generated:** [gamma.app/docs/grb0q0o57lc3f1v](https://gamma.app/docs/grb0q0o57lc3f1v) — the Monopoly rulebook from the demo template, rendered as a professional Blues-themed document in your Gamma account.

---

Here's everything that was built:

**Rulebook → Gamma integration (rebuilt `rulebook-editor.tsx`)**
- **"Sync from project" button** — pulls live data from all upstream tabs: entities → Setup section (grouped by type with descriptions), rules → Actions section (filtered to action-category rules first), players → Turn Order + Objective sections (with victory conditions), research → FAQ section as reference notes. Project title auto-fills the rulebook title.
- **Upstream badges** — shows a live count of how many components, rules, players, and research items are available to sync.
- **"Publish to Gamma" button** (violet, top-right + in Preview tab) — calls the backend `gamma-doc` export endpoint, compiles the full document (all sections + glossary + project metadata), and opens a modal with the formatted markdown, a "Copy document" button, and an "Open Gamma.app" link. The flow is: copy → Gamma.app → New → Paste → Generate.
- **Section cards** now show a green ✓ badge when filled, and have a left border color matched to section type.

**Backend — new `gamma-doc` export kind** (`exports.ts`)
- Gathers all entities (grouped by type), rules (grouped by category with edge cases), players (with victory conditions and special abilities), and compiles a rich structured Monopoly-style markdown document. Handles empty states gracefully with placeholder text for unfilled sections.

**Schema + API types** — added `"gamma-doc"` to the zod enum (`api-zod`), the generated client function signature, and the dist `.d.ts` declarations so TypeScript resolves it cleanly.

**Learn topics — full update** (`learnTopics.ts`)
- `bible:welcome` — now covers all game types, Monopoly demo template, and Complexity Score
- `bible:overview` — documents Complexity Score widget, Monopoly loader, and upstream/downstream tab flow
- `bible:research` — notes that research items appear in Rulebook sync
- `bible:entities` — comprehensive coverage of all 13 component types, Card Studio, Die Face Designer, Variant Manager, Sheet view, BOM view, Zone topology
- `bible:players` — notes upstream connection to Rulebook Editor and Complexity Score
- `bible:rules` — covers Rulebook Editor (Outline/Glossary/Preview tabs), Sync from project, Publish to Gamma workflow
- `bible:assets` — covers BOM view, three-way toggle, manufacturing tier table, CSV export
- `bible:exports` — all 7 export formats including Player Aid and Component BOM, plus Gamma publishing path
- `design101:04-components` — extended with all new component types, tools, and BOM
- **4 new topics added**: `tools:card-studio`, `tools:die-face-designer`, `tools:variant-manager`, `tools:zone-topology`

630	// Smart linker — word-boundary, case-insensitive matching with min name length.
631	// ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

634	function escapeRegex(s: string) {
635	  return s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&");
636	}
637	
638	type LinkMaps = {
639	  entityToRules: Map<number, Set<number>>;
640	  ruleToEntities: Map<number, Set<number>>;
641	};
642	
643	function buildLinks(entities: Entity[], rules: Rule[]): LinkMaps {
644	  const entityToRules = new Map<number, Set<number>>();
645	  const ruleToEntities = new Map<number, Set<number>>();
646	  for (const e of entities) entityToRules.set(e.id, new Set());
647	  for (const r of rules) ruleToEntities.set(r.id, new Set());
648	
649	  const candidates = entities
650	    .filter((e) => e.name && e.name.trim().length >= 3)
651	    .map((e) => ({
652	      id: e.id,
653	      re: new RegExp(
654	        `(?:^|[^A-Za-z0-9_])${escapeRegex(e.name)}(?=[^A-Za-z0-9_]|$)`,
655	        "i",
656	      ),
657	    }));
658	
659	  for (const r of rules) {
660	    const text = `${r.title ?? ""}\n${r.content ?? ""}`;
661	    for (const c of candidates) {
662	      if (c.re.test(text)) {
663	        entityToRules.get(c.id)!.add(r.id);
664	        ruleToEntities.get(r.id)!.add(c.id);
665	      }
666	    }
667	  }
668	  return { entityToRules, ruleToEntities };
669	}

915	// Entity graph — radial SVG, sectored by type
916	// ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
917	type GraphNode = { id: number; name: string; type: string; x: number; y: number; r: number };
918	type GraphEdge = { a: number; b: number; kind: "explicit" | "inferred"; weight: number };
919	
920	function buildGraph(
921	  entities: Entity[],
922	  links: LinkMaps,
923	  width: number,
924	  height: number,
925	): { nodes: GraphNode[]; edges: GraphEdge[] } {
926	  if (entities.length === 0) return { nodes: [], edges: [] };
927	
928	  const groups = new Map<string, Entity[]>();
929	  for (const t of ALL_COMPONENT_TYPES) groups.set(t, []);
930	  for (const e of entities) {
931	    if (!groups.has(e.type)) groups.set(e.type, []);
932	    groups.get(e.type)!.push(e);
933	  }
934	  const filledGroups = [...groups.entries()].filter(([, arr]) => arr.length > 0);
935	
936	  const cx = width / 2;
937	  const cy = height / 2;
938	  const radius = Math.min(width, height) / 2 - 60;
939	
940	  const total = entities.length;
941	  let angleCursor = -Math.PI / 2;
942	  const placement = new Map<number, { x: number; y: number }>();
943	
944	  for (const [, arr] of filledGroups) {
945	    const arcSize = (arr.length / total) * 2 * Math.PI;
946	    const step = arcSize / arr.length;
947	    for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
948	      const angle = angleCursor + step * i + step / 2;
949	      placement.set(arr[i].id, {
950	        x: cx + Math.cos(angle) * radius,
951	        y: cy + Math.sin(angle) * radius,
952	      });
953	    }
954	    angleCursor += arcSize;
955	  }
956	
957	  const nodes: GraphNode[] = entities.map((e) => {
958	    const ruleCount = links.entityToRules.get(e.id)?.size ?? 0;
959	    const r = 8 + Math.min(8, Math.log2(1 + ruleCount) * 3);
960	    const pos = placement.get(e.id)!;
961	    return { id: e.id, name: e.name, type: e.type, x: pos.x, y: pos.y, r };
962	  });
963	
964	  const edges: GraphEdge[] = [];
965	  const seen = new Set<string>();
966	  const key = (a: number, b: number) => (a < b ? `${a}:${b}` : `${b}:${a}`);
967	
968	  const nameIndex = new Map<string, number>();
969	  for (const e of entities) nameIndex.set(e.name.toLowerCase(), e.id);
970	
971	  for (const e of entities) {
972	    if (!e.relatedTo) continue;
973	    const refs = e.relatedTo.split(/[,;\n]/).map((s) => s.trim()).filter(Boolean);
974	    for (const ref of refs) {
975	      const targetId = nameIndex.get(ref.toLowerCase());
976	      if (!targetId || targetId === e.id) continue;
977	      const k = key(e.id, targetId);
978	      if (seen.has(k)) continue;
979	      seen.add(k);
980	      edges.push({ a: e.id, b: targetId, kind: "explicit", weight: 1 });
981	    }
982	  }
983	
984	  const coCount = new Map<string, number>();
985	  for (const ruleEntities of links.ruleToEntities.values()) {
986	    const arr = [...ruleEntities];
987	    for (let i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
988	      for (let j = i + 1; j < arr.length; j++) {
989	        const k = key(arr[i], arr[j]);
990	        coCount.set(k, (coCount.get(k) ?? 0) + 1);
991	      }
992	    }
993	  }
994	  for (const [k, count] of coCount.entries()) {
995	    if (count < 2) continue;
996	    if (seen.has(k)) continue;
997	    seen.add(k);
998	    const [a, b] = k.split(":").map(Number);
999	    edges.push({ a, b, kind: "inferred", weight: count });
1000	  }
1001	
1002	  return { nodes, edges };
1003	}

1264	          </div>
1265	          {rows.length === 0 ? (
1266	            <p className="text-xs text-muted-foreground p-4">No components match.</p>
1267	          ) : (
1268	            rows.map(({ entity: e, propCount, ruleCount }) => (
1269	              <button
1270	                key={e.id}
1271	                onClick={() => onJump("entities")}
1272	                className="w-full grid grid-cols-12 gap-3 px-3 py-2 items-center text-sm hover:bg-muted/10 cursor-pointer text-left border-b border-border/40 last:border-0 transition-colors"
1273	                data-testid={`browser-row-${e.id}`}
1274	              >
1275	                <div className="col-span-4 truncate">
1276	                  <span className="text-white font-medium">{e.name}</span>
1277	                  {e.subtype && <span className="text-muted-foreground text-xs ml-1.5">/ {e.subtype}</span>}
1278	                </div>
1279	                <div className="col-span-2">
1280	                  <Badge variant="outline" className={`text-[10px] ${typeBadge(e.type)}`}>{e.type}</Badge>
1281	                </div>
1282	                <div className="col-span-1 text-xs text-muted-foreground font-mono">{propCount}</div>
1283	                <div className={`col-span-1 text-xs font-mono ${ruleCount === 0 ? "text-amber-400/70" : "text-muted-foreground"}`}>
1284	                  {ruleCount}
1285	                </div>
1286	                <div className="col-span-4 flex flex-wrap gap-1">
1287	                  {e.description && <span className="text-[10px] px-1.5 py-0.5 rounded bg-muted/30 text-muted-foreground">desc</span>}
1288	                  {e.lore && <span className="text-[10px] px-1.5 py-0.5 rounded bg-purple-500/10 text-purple-400">lore</span>}
1289	                  {e.designNotes && <span className="text-[10px] px-1.5 py-0.5 rounded bg-blue-500/10 text-blue-400">notes</span>}
1290	                  {e.stats && <span className="text-[10px] px-1.5 py-0.5 rounded bg-green-500/10 text-green-400">stats</span>}
1291	                  {!e.description && !e.lore && !e.designNotes && !e.stats && (
1292	                    <span className="text-[10px] text-muted-foreground/50 italic">empty</span>
1293	                  )}
1294	                </div>
1295	              </button>
1296	            ))
1297	          )}
1298	        </div>
1299	      </CardContent>
1300	    </Card>
1301	  );
1302	}

1304	// ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
1305	// Property dictionary — live view of project's actual properties
1306	// ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
1307	function PropertyDictionary({
1308	  entities, properties,
1309	}: {
1310	  entities: Entity[];
1311	  properties: EntityProp[];
1312	}) {
1313	  const entityById = useMemo(() => new Map(entities.map((e) => [e.id, e])), [entities]);
1314	
1315	  const dict = useMemo(() => {
1316	    const byName = new Map<string, { name: string; types: Set<string>; entities: Entity[] }>();
1317	    for (const p of properties) {
1318	      const ent = entityById.get(p.entityId);
1319	      if (!ent) continue;
1320	      const entry = byName.get(p.name) ?? { name: p.name, types: new Set(), entities: [] };
1321	      entry.types.add(p.dataType);
1322	      entry.entities.push(ent);
1323	      byName.set(p.name, entry);
1324	    }
1325	    return [...byName.values()].sort((a, b) => b.entities.length - a.entities.length);
1326	  }, [properties, entityById]);
1327	
1328	  return (
1329	    <Card>
1330	      <CardHeader>
1331	        <CardTitle className="flex items-center gap-2 text-base">
1332	          <Layers className="h-4 w-4" /> Live property dictionary
1333	          <Badge variant="outline" className="text-[10px] ml-1">{dict.length}</Badge>
1334	        </CardTitle>
1335	        <CardDescription>
1336	          Properties your project components actually have, grouped by name. Mixed data-types or near-duplicate names (<code>hp</code> vs <code>health</code>) are usually worth normalizing.
1337	        </CardDescription>
1338	      </CardHeader>
1339	      <CardContent>
1340	        {dict.length === 0 ? (
1341	          <p className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">No component properties yet. Add properties to entities to populate this dictionary.</p>
1342	        ) : (
1343	          <div className="space-y-2 max-h-[420px] overflow-y-auto pr-2">
1344	            {dict.map((d) => (
1345	              <div key={d.name} className="border border-border/60 rounded-md p-2.5 bg-background/30" data-testid={`prop-dict-${d.name}`}>
1346	                <div className="flex items-center gap-2 flex-wrap">
1347	                  <code className="text-sm text-white font-mono font-semibold">{d.name}</code>
1348	                  {[...d.types].map((t) => (
1349	                    <Badge key={t} variant="outline"
1350	                      className={`text-[10px] font-mono ${d.types.size > 1 ? "bg-amber-500/10 text-amber-400 border-amber-500/30" : "bg-secondary/30"}`}>
1351	                      {t}
1352	                    </Badge>
1353	                  ))}
1354	                  <span className="text-xs text-muted-foreground ml-auto">
1355	                    {d.entities.length} {d.entities.length === 1 ? "component" : "components"}
1356	                  </span>
1357	                </div>
1358	                <div className="flex flex-wrap gap-1 mt-1.5">
1359	                  {d.entities.map((e) => (
1360	                    <span key={e.id} className={`text-[10px] px-1.5 py-0.5 rounded border ${typeBadge(e.type)}`} title={`${e.type}: ${e.name}`}>
1361	                      {e.name}
1362	                    </span>
1363	                  ))}
1364	                </div>
1365	                {d.types.size > 1 && (
1366	                  <p className="text-[11px] text-amber-400/80 mt-1.5 italic">
1367	                    ⚠ Mixed data-types — components define <code>{d.name}</code> with different types.
1368	                  </p>
1369	                )}
1370	              </div>
1371	            ))}
1372	          </div>
1373	        )}
1374	      </CardContent>
1375	    </Card>
1376	  );
1377	}
1378	
1379	// ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
1380	// Rule ↔ component links list
1381	// ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
1382	function RuleEntityLinks({
1383	  rules, entities, links,
1384	}: {
1385	  rules: Rule[];
1386	  entities: Entity[];
1387	  links: LinkMaps;
1388	}) {

1390	  const linked = useMemo(() => {
1391	    return rules
1392	      .map((r) => ({
1393	        rule: r,
1394	        entityIds: [...(links.ruleToEntities.get(r.id) ?? new Set<number>())],
1395	      }))
1396	      .filter((x) => x.entityIds.length > 0);
1397	  }, [rules, links]);
1398	
1399	  return (
1400	    <Card>
1401	      <CardHeader>
1402	        <CardTitle className="flex items-center gap-2 text-base">
1403	          <LinkIcon className="h-4 w-4" /> Rule ↔ Component links
1404	          <Badge variant="outline" className="text-[10px] ml-1">{linked.length}</Badge>
1405	        </CardTitle>
1406	        <CardDescription>
1407	          Whole-word, case-insensitive matches between rule text and component names.
1408	        </CardDescription>
1409	      </CardHeader>
1410	      <CardContent>
1411	        {linked.length === 0 ? (
1412	          <p className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">
1413	            No detected links yet. Reference component names in rules to populate this list.
1414	          </p>
1415	        ) : (
1416	          <div className="space-y-3 max-h-[500px] overflow-y-auto pr-2">
1417	            {linked.map(({ rule, entityIds }) => (
1418	              <div key={rule.id} className="border-l-2 border-primary/40 pl-3 py-1">
1419	                <div className="font-medium text-sm">{rule.title}</div>
1420	                <div className="flex flex-wrap gap-1 mt-1">
1421	                  {entityIds.map((id) => {
1422	                    const e = entityById.get(id);
1423	                    if (!e) return null;
1424	                    return (
1425	                      <span key={id} className={`text-[10px] px-1.5 py-0.5 rounded border ${typeBadge(e.type)}`}>
1426	                        {e.name}
1427	                      </span>
1428	                    );
1429	                  })}
1430	                </div>
1431	              </div>
1432	            ))}
1433	          </div>

1437	  );
1438	}

1440	// ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

1443	export function Ontology({
1444	  projectId, onJump,

1452

1454	  const rls = rules ?? [];
1455	  const props = properties ?? [];
1456	  const goTo = onJump ?? (() => {});
1457	
1458	  const links = useMemo(() => buildLinks(ents, rls), [ents, rls]);
1459

1461	    const m = new Map<number, EntityProp[]>();
1462	    for (const p of props) {
1463	      const arr = m.get(p.entityId) ?? [];
1464	      arr.push(p);
1465	      m.set(p.entityId, arr);
1466	    }
1467	    return m;

1469

1471	    const out: Record<string, Entity[]> = {};
1472	    for (const e of ents) {
1473	      const key = e.type || "other";
1474	      if (!out[key]) out[key] = [];
1475	      out[key].push(e);
1476	    }
1477	    return out;

1481

1483	    <div className="space-y-8 max-w-6xl pb-8">

1490	        </p>
1491	      </div>
1492	
1493	      {isLoading ? (
1494	        <Skeleton className="h-40" />
1495	      ) : (
1496	        <>
1497	          {/* 1. Coverage gaps */}
1498	          <section>

1500	          </section>
1501	
1502	          {/* 2. Visual graph */}

1505	          </section>
1506

1510	          </section>
1511	
1512	          {/* 4. Live property dictionary + rule links side by side */}
1513	          <section>
1514	            <h3 className="text-sm font-bold uppercase tracking-wider text-muted-foreground mb-3 flex items-center gap-1.5">
1515	              <Activity className="h-3.5 w-3.5" /> Connections
1516	            </h3>
1517	            <div className="grid grid-cols-1 lg:grid-cols-2 gap-4">
1518	              <Card>
1519	                <CardHeader>
1520	                  <CardTitle className="flex items-center gap-2 text-base">
1521	                    <Box className="h-4 w-4" /> Component taxonomy
1522	                  </CardTitle>
1523	                  <CardDescription>Grouped by type.</CardDescription>
1524	                </CardHeader>
1525	                <CardContent>
1526	                  {!ents.length ? (
1527	                    <p className="text-sm text-muted-foreground">No components yet.</p>
1528	                  ) : (
1529	                    <div className="space-y-4">
1530	                      {Object.entries(groupedEntities).map(([kind, list]) => (
1531	                        <div key={kind}>
1532	                          <div className="flex items-center gap-2 mb-2">
1533	                            <span className={`text-[10px] font-bold uppercase tracking-wider px-1.5 py-0.5 rounded border ${typeBadge(kind)}`}>{kind}</span>

1535	                          </div>
1536	                          <div className="flex flex-wrap gap-1.5">
1537	                            {list.map((e) => (
1538	                              <Badge
1539	                                key={e.id}
1540	                                variant="outline"
1541	                                className="text-xs bg-primary/10 border-primary/20 text-primary cursor-pointer hover:bg-primary/20"
1542	                                onClick={() => goTo("entities")}
1543	                              >
1544	                                {e.name}
1545	                              </Badge>
1546	                            ))}
1547	                          </div>
1548	                        </div>
1549	                      ))}
1550	                    </div>
1551	                  )}
1552	                </CardContent>
1553	              </Card>
1554	
1555	              <RuleEntityLinks rules={rls} entities={ents} links={links} />
1556	            </div>
1557	          </section>
1558	
1559	          {/* 5. Live property dictionary */}
1560	          <section>
1561	            <PropertyDictionary entities={ents} properties={props} />
1562	          </section>
1563	
1564	          {/* 6. Property Glossary — static canonical reference */}
1565	          <section>
1566	            <PropertyGlossary />
1567	          </section>
1568	
1569	          {/* 7. Coverage stats */}
1570	          <Card>
1571	            <CardHeader>
1572	              <CardTitle className="flex items-center gap-2 text-base">
1573	                <Activity className="h-4 w-4" /> Coverage stats
1574	              </CardTitle>

1601	                    <ComponentTypeReference key={t} type={t} />

1614	                </div>

1616	            </div>
1617	          </section>

1620	    </div>

1629	    </div>

import { useMemo, useState } from "react";
import {
  useListEntities,
  useListRules,
  useListProjectEntityProperties,
  type Entity,
  type Rule,
  type EntityProperty,
} from "@workspace/api-client-react";
import {
  Network, Box, Activity, Link as LinkIcon, ChevronDown, ChevronRight,
  Lightbulb, BookOpen, AlertTriangle, GitBranch, Table as TableIcon,
  Layers, ArrowRight, Search, Sparkles, Library,
} from "lucide-react";
import { Card, CardContent, CardHeader, CardTitle, CardDescription } from "@/components/ui/card";
import { Skeleton } from "@/components/ui/skeleton";
import { Badge } from "@/components/ui/badge";
import { Input } from "@/components/ui/input";
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";

// ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// Component type system — 12 canonical types in two groups
// ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
type ComponentDoc = {
  color: string;
  border: string;
  bg: string;
  badge: string;
  hex: string;
  icon: string;
  tagline: string;
  what: string;
  ideas: string[];
  properties: { name: string; type: string; note: string }[];
  designTip: string;
};

const PHYSICAL_TYPES = ["Card", "Deck", "Token", "Die", "Tile", "Meeple", "Board"] as const;
const WORLD_TYPES = ["Location", "Faction", "Event", "Resource", "Ability"] as const;
const ALL_COMPONENT_TYPES = [...PHYSICAL_TYPES, ...WORLD_TYPES] as const;
type ComponentType = typeof ALL_COMPONENT_TYPES[number];

const COMPONENT_DOCS: Record<ComponentType, ComponentDoc> = {
  Card: {
    color: "text-violet-400",
    border: "border-violet-500/30",
    bg: "bg-violet-500/5",
    badge: "bg-violet-500/20 text-violet-400 border-violet-500/30",
    hex: "#7c3aed",
    icon: "🃏",
    tagline: "Individual playable cards drawn from a hand or deck.",
    what: "Cards are the primary interaction medium in card-driven games. Each card is a discrete unit of choice — playing, holding, or discarding it creates tension, planning, and hand management decisions. The composition of your hand at any moment defines your options.",
    ideas: [
      "Action Card — Play for an immediate effect or bonus",
      "Item Card — Equip for persistent stat boosts",
      "Spell Card — One-time powerful effect, often costly",
      "Encounter Card — Drawn from a deck, reactive surprise",
      "Quest Card — Long-term objective with staged rewards",
      "Treasure Card — Loot with varying rarity and effects",
      "Attack / Defense Card — Played in combat as reactions",
    ],
    properties: [
      { name: "cost", type: "number", note: "Resources or action points to play this card" },
      { name: "power", type: "number", note: "Offensive value in combat resolution" },
      { name: "defense", type: "number", note: "Damage mitigation when played defensively" },
      { name: "effect_type", type: "enum", note: "buff / debuff / damage / heal / draw / discard" },
      { name: "trigger", type: "string", note: "Condition under which the effect fires" },
      { name: "rarity", type: "enum", note: "common / uncommon / rare / legendary" },
      { name: "hand_cost", type: "number", note: "Additional cards discarded to play this" },
    ],
    designTip:
      "Cards with dual modes (play for effect A or discard for effect B) multiply decisions without adding rules complexity. Control how many copies exist per deck — scarcity drives tension.",
  },
  Deck: {
    color: "text-indigo-400",
    border: "border-indigo-500/30",
    bg: "bg-indigo-500/5",
    badge: "bg-indigo-500/20 text-indigo-400 border-indigo-500/30",
    hex: "#4f46e5",
    icon: "📦",
    tagline: "An ordered or shuffled collection of cards players draw from.",
    what: "Decks are the supply source for card interactions. They create uncertainty (what's coming next?), pacing, and depletion tension. A thinning deck or a freshly shuffled one each produce distinct strategic feelings — the state of the deck IS information.",
    ideas: [
      "Action Deck — Core decision cards for the active player",
      "Event Deck — World events triggered each round",
      "Encounter Deck — Enemies or challenges drawn on entry",
      "Spell / Magic Deck — Drawn by caster characters only",
      "Loot Deck — Rewards drawn after clearing a room",
      "Market Deck — Purchasable upgrades available each turn",
    ],
    properties: [
      { name: "size", type: "number", note: "Total cards at game start" },
      { name: "cards_per_draw", type: "number", note: "Cards drawn per action" },
      { name: "shuffle_when_empty", type: "boolean", note: "Reshuffle discard pile to refill?" },
      { name: "shared", type: "boolean", note: "One deck for all vs. per-player deck?" },
      { name: "visible_top", type: "boolean", note: "Top card visible to all players?" },
      { name: "discard_visible", type: "boolean", note: "Discard pile face-up and inspectable?" },
    ],
    designTip:
      "Deck thickness controls information density. Thin decks (10–15 cards) cycle fast and feel predictable — ideal for engine-builders. Thick decks (40+) feel like a lottery — right for randomness-heavy themes.",
  },
  Token: {
    color: "text-amber-400",
    border: "border-amber-500/30",
    bg: "bg-amber-500/5",
    badge: "bg-amber-500/20 text-amber-400 border-amber-500/30",
    hex: "#d97706",
    icon: "🪙",
    tagline: "Physical markers tracking resources, status, or quantities on the board.",
    what: "Tokens are the economy's heartbeat — they track health, currency, influence, and any countable game state. The act of gaining and losing tokens is often the most tactile and satisfying core loop. Supply scarcity (running out of tokens) creates natural hard limits.",
    ideas: [
      "Health / Hit Points — Damage tracker per unit",
      "Gold / Coin — Spend on actions or purchases",
      "Victory Points — Accumulate for end-game scoring",
      "Status Marker — Poisoned, Burning, Stunned",
      "Influence Chip — Political or social power",
      "Food / Supply — Upkeep consumed each round",
      "Action Token — Placed to mark a used action",
    ],
    properties: [
      { name: "quantity", type: "number", note: "Total supply in the game box" },
      { name: "max_stack", type: "number", note: "Max per player or per space" },
      { name: "per_player", type: "boolean", note: "Each player has own supply?" },
      { name: "tradeable", type: "boolean", note: "Can players exchange freely?" },
      { name: "stackable", type: "boolean", note: "Can multiples share one space?" },
      { name: "value", type: "number", note: "Point or trade value per token" },
    ],
    designTip:
      "Keep tokens physically distinct — different shapes or colors prevent confusion during high-tension plays. Soft caps (max 10 gold) create interesting spend pressure before the cap hits.",
  },
  Die: {

const FALLBACK_HEX = "#7c3aed";

function typeBadge(type: string) {
  const doc = COMPONENT_DOCS[type as ComponentType];
  return doc?.badge ?? "bg-gray-500/20 text-gray-400 border-gray-500/30";
}

function typeHex(type: string): string {
  return COMPONENT_DOCS[type as ComponentType]?.hex ?? FALLBACK_HEX;
}

// ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// Smart linker — word-boundary, case-insensitive matching with min name length.
// ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
type EntityProp = EntityProperty;

function escapeRegex(s: string) {
  return s.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, "\\$&");
}

type LinkMaps = {
  entityToRules: Map<number, Set<number>>;
  ruleToEntities: Map<number, Set<number>>;
};

function buildLinks(entities: Entity[], rules: Rule[]): LinkMaps {
  const entityToRules = new Map<number, Set<number>>();
  const ruleToEntities = new Map<number, Set<number>>();
  for (const e of entities) entityToRules.set(e.id, new Set());
  for (const r of rules) ruleToEntities.set(r.id, new Set());

  const candidates = entities
    .filter((e) => e.name && e.name.trim().length >= 3)
    .map((e) => ({
      id: e.id,
      re: new RegExp(
        `(?:^|[^A-Za-z0-9_])${escapeRegex(e.name)}(?=[^A-Za-z0-9_]|$)`,
        "i",
      ),
    }));

  for (const r of rules) {
    const text = `${r.title ?? ""}\n${r.content ?? ""}`;
    for (const c of candidates) {
      if (c.re.test(text)) {
        entityToRules.get(c.id)!.add(r.id);
        ruleToEntities.get(r.id)!.add(c.id);
      }
    }
  }
  return { entityToRules, ruleToEntities };
}
